identity.title: Multi-agent Architecture Search via Agentic Supernet

problem.claim: Automate multi-agent system design while allocating inference resources according to each query’s difficulty and domain.

gap.claim: Existing automated workflow methods generally target static, complex, one-size-fits-all systems that do not dynamically allocate resources per query.

contributions.claim: Introduces MaAS, which samples query-dependent agentic systems from a probabilistic, continuous distribution of agentic architectures called an agentic supernet.
Targets tailored allocation of LLM calls, tool calls, and token cost across queries.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their approach by optimizing an agentic supernet rather than pursuing a monolithic agentic system.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report evaluation on six benchmarks showing MaAS uses 6–45% of the inference costs of existing handcrafted or automated multi-agent systems.
The authors report that MaAS surpasses those systems by 0.54%–11.82%.
The authors report superior cross-dataset and cross-LLM-backbone transferability.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-agent systems extend individual-agent capabilities through collaboration, but manual construction is labor-intensive.
Automated workflow methods typically produce static, one-size-fits-all systems that cannot adapt resource allocation to query characteristics.
The paper proposes optimizing a probabilistic continuous agentic supernet and introduces MaAS to sample query-dependent systems with tailored resource use.
Across six benchmarks, the authors report lower inference costs, higher performance, and stronger transferability than existing systems.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a limitation in static system design to a specific remedy: sampling query-dependent architectures with tailored resource allocation.

lessons.interpretation: A strong abstract can align the proposed mechanism directly with the stated failure mode.
lessons.application: When presenting an adaptive system, explicitly map each design choice to the fixed behavior or resource mismatch it is intended to address.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when adaptation is not central to the task or when the system’s operating conditions are genuinely uniform.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the six benchmarks, baselines, task domains, or evaluation protocol.
The meanings of the reported performance margin, inference-cost accounting, and transferability comparisons are unspecified.
No details are given about training cost, sampling procedure, or statistical uncertainty.
